title: Draw the products from their molecular formulas
asks: A reaction gives two products whose molecular formulas are given. Draw each.

know.h: Each {{SN2}} reaction makes one bond from the nucleophile to carbon and breaks one bond from carbon to the leaving group. A dihalide can do this twice, once at each end. A dinucleophile can do it twice, once with each charged atom.

Write each piece as a formula. The piece from a dihalide is its carbon chain (1,2-diiodoethane gives {{C2H4}} plus two iodines). The piece from the nucleophile is everything except its sodium ions (ethane-1,2-dithiolate is {{C2H4S2}}).
Count the halogens in the product formula. Each halogen still present is one end of a dihalide that has not reacted. No halogen means every end has reacted.
Count the nucleophile atoms (S, O or N) in the formula to find how many nucleophile pieces the product contains, and count carbons to find how many dihalide pieces.
One dihalide plus one dinucleophile with no halogen left is a ring. The second {{SN2}} is intramolecular. On the exam: {{C4H8S2}} is 1,4-dithiane.
Two halogens left and one dinucleophile is an open chain with the dinucleophile in the middle and a dihalide piece on each end. On the exam: {{C6H12S2I2}} is {{ICH2CH2SCH2CH2SCH2CH2I}}.
Hydrogens do not change in an {{SN2}} reaction with an anion. Every {{CH2}} stays a {{CH2}}. If a drawing has lost or gained hydrogens, or has a C=C, it is wrong for this kind of question.

Ring size is the number of atoms in the nucleophile piece from one charged atom to the other, plus the carbons of the dihalide from one halogen to the other. S-C-C-S (4) plus C-C (2) is a six-membered ring. Five- and six-membered rings close easily.

Thiolates are excellent nucleophiles and weak bases ({{HS-}} 126,000; a thiol has {{pKa}} about 10.5), and primary iodides and bromides are the best {{SN2}} substrates, so these reactions are clean substitutions with no elimination.

Know which atom attacks. Cyanide and acetylide attack with carbon, so each substitution adds carbons to the chain. Azide adds three nitrogens. Sulfide ({{S^2-}}) has two charges on one atom and can bond to two carbons.

Two equivalents of a nucleophile with one charge replace both halogens and give an open chain. One equivalent replaces one halogen. No ring can form, because each nucleophile is used up after one bond.

The ratio of the reagents decides the open-chain product. Excess dihalide leaves a halogen on each end. Excess dinucleophile leaves a nucleophile atom on each end, which an acid workup turns into S-H or O-H.

Skill: after drawing, count C, H and every other atom of your structure and compare with the formula given. Only C-nucleophile bonds are made: never S-S, O-O or a bond between two carbons of different pieces (unless the nucleophile is a carbon anion).

method: Write the formula of each piece: the carbon chain of the dihalide, and the nucleophile without its counter-ions.
For each product formula, count the halogens left and the nucleophile atoms, and work out how many of each piece it contains. Check that the carbons and hydrogens add up.
Remember what one {{SN2}} does: one C-X bond becomes one C-nucleophile bond, and nothing else changes.
If no halogen is left and there is one of each piece, join both ends: draw the ring and count its atoms.
If halogens are left, put the nucleophile piece in the middle and a dihalide piece on each end (or the reverse if nucleophile atoms are left over).
Count the atoms of each drawing against its formula before moving on.

pitfalls.h: Stopping after one substitution and never asking what the second charged atom does. It attacks again: the same chain (a ring) or a second molecule (a chain).
Drawing an S-S or O-O bond to make the formula fit. {{SN2}} at carbon makes only bonds from the nucleophile to carbon.
Changing the number of hydrogens: drawing a C=C, or adding H to a sulfur that has already bonded twice.
Drawing an isomeric ring with the right formula but the wrong connections, for example both sulfurs on one carbon when they came from a two-carbon dihalide.
Forgetting that cyanide and acetylide bring their own carbons into the product.
Drawing two separate small molecules for one formula. A molecular formula describes one molecule.
